lesson.title: The Mirror Line: Axis of Symmetry
lesson.summary: The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through a parabola's vertex, and every point on one side of it has a mirror-image twin at the same height on the other side.
lesson.body:
A parabola is symmetric, and that symmetry happens across a specific vertical line called the axis of symmetry. This line always passes straight through the vertex, splitting the parabola into two halves that are exact mirror images of each other.

Because the axis passes through the vertex, it uses the same x-value: for a quadratic in standard form f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, the axis of symmetry is the vertical line x = -b/(2a). For f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3, you already found in the last section that the vertex is (2, -1), so the axis of symmetry is the line x = 2.

You can see this mirroring directly in the table of values from a couple sections ago: (0, 3) and (4, 3) sit the same distance, 2 units, on either side of x = 2, and both produce the same output, 3. Likewise (1, 0) and (3, 0) sit 1 unit on either side of x = 2, and both produce 0. That is not a coincidence, it is what symmetry across x = 2 guarantees: any two x-values that are equally spaced from the axis on opposite sides will always produce the same y-value.

This is genuinely useful, not just a nice pattern. Once you know the axis of symmetry, you only need to calculate points on one side of the parabola, then reflect them across the axis to get the matching points on the other side for free, cutting your work roughly in half. You will rely on exactly this shortcut when graphing quadratics in full later in this chapter.
